content:
As discussed in the opening article of this same issue of the magazine, flood risk is the one that accounts for the largest share of indemnities paid out by the ‘Extraordinary Risk Insurance’ Scheme in Spain[cite: 12]. In the past 25 years, flooding has been the cause behind 69 of every 100 euros paid out in compensation to insured parties by the Consorcio de Compensación de Seguros (CCS) for property damage in Spain[cite: 12]. For purposes of coverage by the CCS, flooding is defined as follows in Rule 2(c) in the Implementing Regulations for the Extraordinary Risk Insurance Scheme: “the inundation of land caused by the direct action of rainwater, meltwater, or waters from lakes with natural outlets, rivers or inlets, or natural surface watercourses through overflow of their natural beds or channels, and coastal ocean wave battering[cite: 12]. Inundations caused by waters from dams, canals, sewage systems, collectors, and other underground channels built by man that burst, break, or malfunction from causes other than extraordinary risks covered by the Consorcio de Compensación de Seguros, or by rain falling directly on the insured risk, or by rainfall runoff collected by rooftops, drainage systems, or courtyards will not be defined as flooding[cite: 12].”
There is a further circumstance that makes the Consorcio de Compensación de Seguros data especially appropriate for studying this peril: the CCS is the only agent in our country that pays compensation for flood damage to insured property[cite: 12]. Wind is a peril shared by private insurers and the CCS, in that the Extraordinary Risk Insurance Scheme compensates for damage only on attainment of the threshold of an atypical cyclonic storm (ACS or TCA for the Spanish), practice ordinarily when the threshold of 120 km/h is passed[cite: 12]. In contrast, there is no threshold for fluvial, pluvial, or coastal flooding, and the CCS is the owner of 100 % of the risk[cite: 12]. For this reason, Extraordinary Risk Insurance Scheme data make up the entire body of data on flood damage to insured property[cite: 12].
The purpose of this article is thus to carry out a spatial analysis of flood risk by province, both because of the size of that peril and because the CCS holds all the insured damage data[cite: 12]. It should be noted that this study based on insured damage data has been limited to fluvial and pluvial flooding; that is, coastal flooding (and wave battering damage) has not been included[cite: 12].
Figure 1. Average annual compensation for fluvial and pluvial flooding (1996-2019).
The first illustration, Figure 1, shows the average annual compensation for flood damage per province over the study period[cite: 12]. This direct graphic representation in itself reveals several noteworthy features: higher levels of damage in the coastal provinces, particularly along the Mediterranean coast and the Bay of Biscay; greater damage in the basins along the largest rivers, especially the Ebro and the Guadalquivir rivers and to a lesser extent the Duero and the Guadiana rivers; plus an accumulation of damage in the region of Madrid[cite: 12].
Figure 2. Physical map of the Iberian Peninsula and the Balearic and Canary Islands.
Let us pause here for a moment to briefly consider the geography of Spain (Figure 2), which encompasses two quite different settings[cite: 12]. The first consists of a peninsula and an archipelago (the Balearic Islands), plus Spain’s autonomous city enclaves in North Africa, together making up an environment partway conditioned by Atlantic, Mediterranean, and continental African influences[cite: 12]. The interaction of these influences and the markedly mountainous terrain that generally tends to be located quite close to the coast, particularly in the case of the Atlantic coast north of Portugal, along the Bay of Biscay, and the entire Mediterranean coast, including the Balearic Islands, gives rise to a patchwork of climates with few equals in Europe and a variety of sizeable repercussions for the hydrographic network[cite: 12]. First of all, the proximity of significant topographical relief to the main source of moisture, the sea, heightens the impact of precipitation in the above-mentioned areas along the Bay of Biscay and the Mediterranean by forcing air masses to rise, which is conducive to condensation and increases the precipitation rate while at the same time blocking oceanic air flows, causing these to be longer lasting and resulting in greater accumulation[cite: 12]. The small space available between the mountains and the sea means that river courses tend to be short, with steep slopes (and in the case of the Mediterranean, with highly irregular flow volumes), leaving only short windows for precipitation to accumulate from when it starts to fall to when it is discharged into the river network, in that way exacerbating the problem of flooding[cite: 12]. Only the southwestern part of the peninsula allows oceanic air flows to penetrate inland, contributing to a more even distribution pattern of precipitation[cite: 12].
Most of the large rivers empty into the Atlantic, but the Ebro, the river with the highest average volume of flow in the peninsula, discharges into the Mediterranean, while its headwaters have Atlantic features[cite: 12]. This is why regions like Navarre record some of the highest rates of damage, and accumulated flows in the middle section of the river course also cause extensive damage in provinces like Zaragoza[cite: 12]. Something similar can be said of the mountainous or highland areas that are the source of the tributaries to the middle section of the Guadalquivir River, causing flooding in the provinces of Córdoba, Seville, and Cádiz[cite: 12]. The province of Málaga is affected by similar situations on the other side of the mountains[cite: 12].
Figure 1 distinctly shows that, in absolute terms, the greatest damage is concentrated in the provinces of Alicante, Valencia, and Murcia[cite: 12]. It is here where the effects of the potentially heavy precipitation that usually falls in late summer and early autumn combine with the effects of a very warm sea and inflows of cold air in the mid to upper layers of the atmosphere – the Spanish DANAs, or cut-off lows – and with the orographic effects of tall mountains near the sea and the presence of coastal plains which, while narrow, allow people and economic activities to gather there[cite: 12]. And it is also here where all those watercourses, whether still extant or overrun by human occupation of the land, spill out and can go from dry to carrying large volumes of water in a matter of minutes[cite: 12].
The Canary Islands are the second setting we mentioned above[cite: 12]. This archipelago consists of a group of islands, volcanic in origin, located in subtropical climes off the continent of Africa, part of a larger group of widely scattered islands of similar origin, called Macaronesia[cite: 12]. While as a rule the Canary Islands suffer less flood damage than the rest of the country, their relief features are not so different: high elevations quite near the coast, little time for precipitation to accumulate, and watercourses that can go from dry to full with strong, heavy flows in just a few minutes[cite: 12]. The islands are spared worse problems only because there is less active cyclonic circulation and convection there[cite: 12]. However, major damage has occurred when these conditions have arisen, sometimes as a result of tropical storms or hurricanes, which seem likely to increase in the future[cite: 12].
Figure 3. Population density in Spain. Source: INE [Spain’s National Institute of Statistics], 2011.
A little earlier we mentioned a factor that is just as important as physical geography, namely, human occupation[cite: 12]. Ultimately, when speaking of damage, we are speaking of exposed property, something that is inherently human[cite: 12]. Figure 3 depicts population density in Spain and clearly shows that the country mimics a certain “atomic” structure, with most inhabitants divided between the “nucleus” (Madrid) and the “shell” (the coast, sometimes extending inland, as in Galicia, Catalonia, and Andalusia)[cite: 12]. This is the now-famous notion of “empty Spain”, the prevailing situation in most of the country, which is also reflected in indemnities for damage[cite: 12]. In the islands too, most of the population is concentrated along the coast, clearly discernible, for instance, on Tenerife and Grand Canary Island[cite: 12]. Therefore, an exercise in which the damage for each province is divided by its population to even out the effects of exposure and more accurately determine the level of risk is worthwhile[cite: 12]. The results are illustrated in Figure 4[cite: 12].
Figure 4. Average annual compensation by flood and by population (1996-2019).
Figure 4 shows that certain effects clearly attributable to cumulative exposure dissipate, e.g., in the province of Madrid[cite: 12]. There is a similar effect in Barcelona[cite: 12].
In any case, this map displays a view of real average compensation paid by the CCS per flood over the study period in reference to compensation for damage to insured property only, not to all the damage caused[cite: 12]. It is very hard to ascertain all the damage produced by a disaster[cite: 12]. Another article elsewhere in this same issue of the magazine addresses this problem and how hard it is to account for all damage[cite: 12]. The fact that the data for indemnities for insured damage per flood in Spain all come from a single source, the CCS, simplifies the problem greatly, but still we cannot be sure of the total amount of damage, because not all property is insured[cite: 12]. For certain types of property, for instance, infrastructure, insurance penetration is rather low, because it is owned by governments, which self-insure, that is, any damage that is sustained is repaired by the government itself, charged to the budget[cite: 12]. Nevertheless, the system allows property of this kind to be insured, and in fact certain levels of government, above all local and regional governments, do insure part of their infrastructure[cite: 12]. The CCS estimates that, on the whole, it covers around or somewhat more than half of the total damage caused by flooding[cite: 12]. The main source of this gap in damage coverage is presumably infrastructure, proportionally much more costly than other types of property[cite: 12]. In its annual “Estamos Seguros” reports, the Spanish insurers" association, Unespa, estimates the percentage ratio of primary residences that are insured to the total number of primary residences by region (Autonomous Community)[cite: 12]. These are the only data we can use to obtain a closer approximation to what the total amount of damage would be if all homes were insured[cite: 12]. Nationwide, the proportion of homes insured is around 72 %, though with large fluctuations from 88 % in the Basque Country to 38 % in Ceuta[cite: 12].
We have made a projection of the damage, and the results are shown in Figure 5[cite: 12]. On the basis that 34 % of all indemnities paid under the Exceptional Risk Insurance Scheme is for the category of “homes and condominiums”, if the proportion of insured homes were 100 %, the total damage for this category would be given by the following formula: DMCP = DMP [0.66 + 0.34(1/PR)], where DMCP is the average adjusted per capita damage by province, DMP is the average per capita damage by province, and PR is homeowners insurance penetration in the Autonomous Community where the province in question is located[cite: 12]. We realise that this exercise entails certain problems, such as the fact that some of the homes that are uninsured are probably less expensive than the homes that are insured or that there may sometimes be large differences in insurance take-up among provinces in the same Autonomous Community, but this is as close as we can come to reality[cite: 12]. Namely, about 34 % closer to the actual situation, because insurance penetration in business and industry is still unknown (though we would venture to say that it is as high as or higher than home insurance), and the same holds for infrastructure (distinctly lower)[cite: 12]. In the case of damage to motor vehicles, all motor vehicles in operation are covered, because the Extraordinary Risk Insurance Scheme has been applied to all automotive insurance policies since July 2016, including compulsory civil liability policies only[cite: 12].
Figure 5. Average annual per capita flood damage by province (1996-2019) adjusted by homeowners insurance penetration.
Figure 5 appears to be relatively consistent, notwithstanding the assumptions that have had to be made[cite: 12]. Based on the reworked insured damage data, flood risk is greater in provinces that combine nearness to the sea, substantial relief with short fluvial watercourses and low accumulation times, and plains or valleys densely populated by people[cite: 12]. Thus, Guipúzcoa, Murcia, and Alicante, in that order, report the greatest per capita damage[cite: 12]. To a lesser extent, this is also the case for the rest of the Mediterranean coastal region – except for Granada, for the simple reason that most of the population does not live along the coast but in the metropolitan area of the capital city, and for Barcelona, because its extremely large population brings the average down considerably – and for the provinces of Cádiz, Pontevedra, and Santa Cruz de Tenerife[cite: 12].
Other provinces like Navarre, Huesca, and Lérida also stand out on this map, even though they are more or less distant from the sea[cite: 12]. The reason is the combination of mountains that act to heighten precipitation, watercourses that fill rapidly with water flowing at high energies, and human occupation of fluvial floodplains[cite: 12]. Damage occurs also where high flow volumes accumulate and reach the main river channels, such as in provinces like Córdoba and Zaragoza[cite: 12]. On the whole, the courses of the Ebro and Guadalquivir rivers, and to a lesser extent those of the Duero and Guadiana rivers, stand out rather clearly for this reason[cite: 12].
To conclude, we would point out, just by way of an interesting titbit of information, that according to the data employed and the results of this study, Segovia is the province with the lowest flood risk in Spain[cite: 12].
title: Mapping flood risk in Spain from Extraordinary Risk Insurance Scheme data

content:
Introduction In Greek mythology, the naiads (Naïαδες) were the spirits of small brooks, fountains, wells, springs, and other freshwater courses. Unlike the river gods, naiads were smaller and more adaptable to different forms. The NAIAD project, presented in this article, draws inspiration from this ancient river wisdom to tackle disasters. In particular, it focuses on the prevention and reduction phases of the disaster management cycle, viewing nature not only as part of the problem but also as part of the solution.
The ancient Greeks believed that all the waters of the world formed a single system, percolating from the sea into the earth through caverns and returning back to the sea. This systemic view of risk lies at the core of NAIAD. The approach also focuses on the versatility that nature brings and on understanding the protective role of nature-based solutions (NBS) in buffering risks generated by natural hazards through the development of natural assurance schemes.
Floods cause massive impacts worldwide. Numerous recent examples can be found across Europe (pluvial floods in Copenhagen, the Elbe floods of 2002 and 2013, the Danube floods in 2006, the Maritime Alps in 2015, the Lez River in 2014, the Seine in 2016 and 2018, etc.). Around 90% of natural risks are water-related and are likely to become more frequent and severe as a result of climate change. For instance, climate change is expected to increase damages in France by up to 50% by 2050 (Moncoulon et al. 2018). The Caisse Centrale de Réassurance (CCR) estimates that mean annual insured damages will grow by up to 38%, with 50% related to pluvial flooding and 34% to fluvial flooding respectively.
Climate change is already translating into higher risk levels from natural disasters and their associated damage costs (Lawrynuik 2019). Total reported economic losses from natural disasters in Europe over the 1980–2014 period reached 453 billion euros, of which only 45% was insured (EEA, 2019). Therefore, the (re)insurance sector is a critical actor to participate in, absorb, and evaluate the current and potential contributions of what we have termed Natural Assurance Schemes (NAS). The insurance sector has the opportunity to adopt different roles in loss prevention through NBS (Marchal et al. 2019). Catastrophe models developed by or for (re)insurers are tailored to evaluate the quantification of avoided damages via various preventive measures. This quantification can be complemented by estimating additional co-benefits identified by specialized institutions with expertise in the role of green infrastructure to deliver resilience dividends.
1. Main Objective and Strategic Goals The main objective of the EU-funded NAIAD Project (1) is to develop a more comprehensive conceptual framework to better understand the insurable and assurance value of nature to facilitate natural risk prevention, incorporating nature into the equation not only as a problem but as a solution. NAIAD is funded by the European Commission under the Horizon 2020 program over three and a half years (2017–2020) with a budget of 5 million euros. This brief article presents the main results of developing this conceptual framework and operationalizing the ecosystem assurance value in disaster risk management, placing special emphasis on prevention and avoided damages thanks to nature investments.
The project is coordinated by the Duero River Basin Authority. It formed a consortium of 23 partners from 11 European countries, including 3 universities and research/educational institutes, 8 research centers, 4 small and medium enterprises, 3 public entities with competences in applied research, 2 public bodies with key management competencies (the City of Copenhagen and the Duero River Basin Authority), 2 NGOs, and the French public reinsurer CCR.
The project’s objective aligns fully with the draft EU Adaptation Strategy “Adapting to Climate Change” (2) and the EU Taxonomy on Sustainable Finance document (3) (which includes 68 climate change adaptation activities published in March 2020), contributing to making our societies (and activities) more climate-resilient. NAIAD starts from the assumption that healthy and fully functioning ecosystems can significantly contribute to mitigating extreme hydrological risks and increasing societal resilience in the context of climate change.
Figure 1: Location and main objectives of the NAIAD demos.
To demonstrate the role ecosystems can play in reducing water-related risks (e.g., extreme and frequent events), the project developed what we term “Natural Assurance Schemes” (NAS). The project included 9 demonstration sites across Europe covering different scales: large scale in the Thames Basin (UK), Lower Danube (Romania), or Medina Aquifer (Spain); medium scale in the Lez, Brague (France), and Glinščica (Slovenia) catchments; and city scale in Copenhagen (Denmark), Rotterdam (Netherlands), and Lodz (Poland). These sites face diverse risks, predominantly focused on pluvial and fluvial flooding (Danube, Glinščica, Lez, and Brague), while the Medina Aquifer in Spain is oriented towards drought. Their sizes range from the smallest (a neighborhood in Rotterdam) to the largest (a 250 km stretch of the Lower Danube). They cover urban, peri-urban, and rural environments, using cities, basins, and aquifers as analytical units. Crucially, the demo sites range from completely new cases (such as Romania or Slovenia) to established sites where focus was placed on monitoring the efficiency of adopted natural flood management measures (such as the Lower Thames) rather than developing baseline evaluation frameworks.
With this, the project aims to propose new concepts and approaches to widen the portfolio of available solutions. Conventional infrastructure measures are costly: estimated required investment in water infrastructure over the next 15 years is 22 trillion dollars, representing more than half of the total expected infrastructure investment demand ($41 trillion) (WEF, 2019).
Three strategic goals were identified to achieve the central objective of demonstrating the ecosystem assurance value:
Development of biophysical, social, and economic evaluation tools and methods to provide relevant decision-support and planning frameworks for identifying, co-designing, and stimulating NBS strategies in specific locations. Testing these tools and methods across the 9 real-environment demo sites, providing evidence on ecosystem value for disaster risk reduction (DRR) and ecosystem-based adaptation. Policy uptake and exploitation of project results, engaging decision-makers and legislators across various domains to validate results, identify next implementation steps, and pinpoint knowledge gaps requiring further R&D. After briefly discussing the main conceptual framework, the following sections present the results corresponding to these three strategic goals.
2. Conceptual Framework: Natural Assurance Schemes for Adopting Nature-Based Solutions in Ecological DRR and Ecosystem-Based Adaptation The importance of acting earlier in the risk management cycle to support climate change adaptation and Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR) has become increasingly clear. This involves adopting and standardizing NBS as an alternative or complement to conventional grey solutions to prevent or reduce risks, thereby increasing resilience and response capacity to hydrological hazards.
Interest in NBS has grown significantly in recent years. The European Commission (2015) defines nature-based solutions as those inspired and supported by nature, which are cost-effective, simultaneously provide environmental, social, and economic benefits, and build resilience. NAIAD focused particularly on how NBS can better prepare society and increase resilience against natural hazards, evaluating prevention value in terms of avoided damages and co-benefits: what we term “assurance value”. NBS fulfill multiple functions—from conserving or rehabilitating natural ecosystems to enhancing or developing natural processes in modified/artificial ecosystems—and can be applied at micro-scales (e.g., a small wetland) or macro-scales (e.g., floodplain restoration) (WWAP/UN-Water, 2018).
We established a conceptual distinction starting from the fact that insurance value can have several interpretations or components depending on the value dimension considered—specifically, what is being insured: the ecosystem or human assets? It also depends on the risk type considered. Hence the distinction between financial risk-transfer products (e.g., insuring a mangrove to protect its physical asset value) and the “assurance value of nature” (insuring the protective functions provided by nature itself, whether formally insured or not) (4). Theoretical literature on ecosystem insurance value exists (Pascual et al., 2010; Baümgartner & Strunz, 2014; Bartkovski et al., 2015), but practical operational methods enabling cities or basins to evaluate strategies incorporating NBS against grey alternatives or inaction remain scarce.
A suite of tools and methods was developed—and is briefly presented in this article (5)—designed to capture the natural assurance value in risk reduction provided by natural systems (Marchal et al. 2019) (6). This encompasses a comprehensive range of economic, financial, regulatory, institutional, and stakeholder-engagement mechanisms that regulate a sustainable and equitable flow of co-benefits between NBS and society. The resulting modular, structured approach incorporates (1) methodologies to assess and value NBS biophysically, socially, and economically, (2) risk perception concepts, and (3) implementation experiences across NAIAD case studies to operationalize all elements needed for environmental DRR enablement.
3. Biophysical, Social, and Economic Assessment Tools and Methods The starting point for all demonstration projects was the biophysical assessment of exposure and risk. Several tools and methods were developed, tailored for application across different scales.
3.1. Biophysical Tools and Methods at Different Scales: Eco:Actuary and FEV Tools The Eco:Actuary toolkit was developed for large-scale projects and comprises three main elements: First, the Eco:Actuary Decision Support System, a global catastrophe model mapping flood risk and exposure under present climate conditions and IPCC scenarios, as well as damage mitigation and avoided losses achieved via Natural Flood Management (NFM). Second, //Smart:River autonomous stations (see Figure 2), which utilize low-cost, DIY IoT-connected monitoring stations to track real-time river levels and quantify NFM contributions to flood risk reduction. Third, the Eco:Actuary Investment Planner, a simple spreadsheet-based online tool for evaluating the scale and approximate cost of interventions needed to reach a predefined flood reduction target. The insurance sector is particularly interested in catastrophe models as standard tools to assess risk severity and set appropriate insurance premiums. The Eco:Actuary tool allows users to alter scenarios to explore climate change impacts alongside mitigation options like land-use shifts, territorial management practices, or NFM interventions.
Figure 2: Image of a //Smart:River autonomous station: using IoT for flood prevention.
In several countries, national governments and the insurance industry closely align to boost flood risk reduction awareness. This demonstrates how insurance and risk mitigation interact: by investing in mitigation, insurance companies can significantly lower long-term claim payouts. //Smart uses low-cost IoT water-level logger networks to (a) evaluate mitigation measure effectiveness and (b) monitor extreme peak levels during flood events—serving either as early warning systems or as real-time data feeds for parametric insurance products (where payouts trigger automatically based on predefined thresholds like flood depth).
Methods were also developed for smaller scales, such as the Flood-Excess-Volume (FEV) method and tool, providing rapid cost-effectiveness assessments for flood mitigation strategies. To optimize generic flood mitigation strategies for specific catchments, an algorithmic protocol or “tool” is required that evaluates a wide range of measures in a clear, quantifiable, educational, and user-friendly manner accessible to non-experts. Developed through a collaboration between the University of Leeds (UK) and NAIAD, the tool was tested using real flood event data from the UK, France, and Slovenia (Bokhove et al., 2019, 2020) (see box below for details).
THE “FLOOD-EXCESS-VOLUME” (FEV) TOOL
Piton, G., Tacnet, J.M., Bohove, O., and Kelmanson, L.A.
Optimally, this tool overcomes two main obstacles: First, it identifies and uses quantifiable, easy-to-measure flood severity indicators, making the tool objective, transparent, user-friendly, repeatable, and flexible. Second, it rapidly verifies whether a given set of protection measures is sufficient to mitigate a specified flood severity level.
The required input data are the design flood hydrograph (discharge time series), the stage-discharge rating curve (channel capacity), and the threshold discharge level above which severe flooding occurs.
Using this information, the tool first calculates the Flood-Excess-Volume (FEV)—the total volume of water during a flood event that cannot be contained by existing defenses (Figure Ia). Second, it calculates the dimensions of a virtual 2-meter-deep square lake capable of holding the calculated FEV (Figure Ib). This human-scale visualization helps stakeholders intuitively grasp the excess water volume that must be retained to provide flood protection, contrasting with less intuitive real-world catchment topographies. This simplified visualization empowers a non-expert audience to comprehend required retention volumes.
The final step divides the virtual lake into constituent components associated with specific flood protection measures (Figure Ic), such as restored wetlands, leaky wooden dams, floodplain reconnection, retention basins, or river space restoration.
<p class="caption-text">Figure I: The three stages of FEV analysis. (a) Three-panel graph showing FEV: (bottom-left) river level time series, (top-left) stage-discharge curve, and (top-right) discharge data with FEV represented as the blue area above the threshold discharge. (b) 2m-deep square lake representation facilitating FEV severity visualization. (c) FEV effectiveness evaluation calculated for each measure as an equivalent FEV fraction (adapted from Bokhove et al., 2019).</p>3.2. Participatory Modeling: Converting Obstacles into Opportunities for Collaboration and Collective Action The second methodology focused on social assessment using a participatory modeling tool for co-designing NBS. This method manages risk perception ambiguity by fostering inclusive and balanced stakeholder engagement. Rooted in systems thinking, the model defines and analyzes complex, non-linear causal links influencing system behavior. The tool applies a sequential multi-phase process: i) eliciting and analyzing individual risk perceptions; ii) developing the systems thinking model; iii) detecting main barriers to NBS co-design and implementation; and iv) analyzing trade-offs and identifying conflicts. Phases i and iii allowed NAIAD to involve stakeholders and decision-makers in a co-design process focused on creating effective interventions to mitigate hydrological risks while delivering expected co-benefits. Phase iv methods enhanced equity in NBS implementation. Stakeholders recognized their contributions within the model, developing a sense of ownership over the results. Location-specific indicators were successfully developed and applied in the Glinščica catchment (Santoro et al., 2019; Pagano et al., 2019), Lower Danube (Giordano et al., 2020), and Medina Aquifer (Giordano et al., 2020).
The participatory modeling approach across NAIAD demo sites fostered inclusive, legitimate, and cooperative NAS design, boosting social acceptance of NBS. The modeling tool ensured inclusiveness and legitimacy by giving voice to diverse viewpoints regarding hydrological risk management, prioritizing rich knowledge collection over forced consensus. Cognitive mapping captured individual risk perceptions, local impacts, and social priorities. Integrating local stakeholder insights with scientific data yielded models perceived as legitimate, building strong stakeholder ownership.
Cooperation yielded two key advantages: First, stakeholder engagement built trust and relationships among participants, scientists, and decision-makers. Second, it unraveled complex interaction networks among decision-makers. Results demonstrated that dysfunctional interaction networks represent major barriers to NBS deployment. Consequently, targeted actions boosting institutional and non-institutional cooperation are essential for effective NBS implementation.
In parallel with physical and socioeconomic evaluations conducted by technical partners, local stakeholder meetings were organized across all 9 demo sites. In addition to presenting project goals, public participation sessions enabled local stakeholders to actively collaborate with technical teams on project deliverables (Figure 3).3.3. Integrated Cost-Benefit Analysis of Nature-Based Strategies Economic evaluation is a core component of natural assurance scheme development. A detailed economic evaluation framework was created to compare primary costs and benefits generated by NBS for hydrological risks using monetary valuation methods:
Implementation Costs: Direct expenses required to build and maintain NBS strategies. Opportunity Costs: Losses in economic yield from taking land out of production or reallocating it to NBS instead of profitable uses like commercial/residential development (indirect costs). Avoided Damages: Reduced economic losses resulting from hydrological risk mitigation via NBS (the primary direct benefit). Co-benefits: Additional environmental, economic, and social benefits generated by NBS. Cost-Benefit Analysis (CBA) compares these costs and benefits over project lifespans across grey, hybrid, and NBS alternatives. Results show that NBS implementation costs are lower than grey infrastructure costs for equivalent risk reduction levels, reinforcing NBS cost-effectiveness arguments and encouraging systematic consideration by decision-makers. However, direct flood damage reduction benefits alone may not always fully cover initial capital and maintenance costs—posing challenges for single-sector risk mitigation financing. Comprehensive project designs tapping into all generated co-benefits are required.
Co-benefits (air quality improvement, urban heat island mitigation, landscape enhancement, carbon sequestration) represent the largest share of total value generated by NBS strategies. Integrating co-benefits is essential to make NBS projects economically advantageous. This multiplicity of benefits requires project developers to seek out and blend diverse funding and financing streams, supported by enabling policy frameworks.
To evaluate avoided damages, NAIAD leveraged CCR’s expertise using their Catastrophe (CAT) Model. The first unit models flood overflow and surface runoff hazards; the second geolocates insured property contracts at address-level with risk type and insured values; the third combines hazard intensity and exposure vulnerability via damage curves linking water stage/flow to structural damage rates. Ultimately, insured disaster losses are calculated in monetary terms (see CAT Model box).
COST-BENEFIT ANALYSIS OF NATURE-BASED SOLUTIONS USING INSURANCE TOOLS: THE CAT MODEL
Marchal, R. and Moncoulon, D.
Caisse Centrale de Réassurance (CCR), the French state reinsurer, collaborated with researchers from INRAE, BRGM, and the University of Nice within NAIAD to quantify NBS loss prevention roles and support local decision-making. CCR applied its CAT model to simulate flood events, evaluate hazards, and quantify avoided damages, incorporating climate change projections (Moncoulon et al., 2018).
CCR models direct tangible damages (floods, earthquakes, storm surges) under the French Natural Catastrophes Compensation Scheme. The CAT model combines hazard, vulnerability, and damage modules (Figure II). Overflow and runoff hazards are simulated via a 2D distributed model at 25m resolution calibrated nationally (Moncoulon et al., 2014).
The methodology was customized for French demo catchments and historic flood events by: 1. Collecting local land-use data; 2. Adjusting Digital Terrain Model (DTM) slope calculations to track grid-level water depth along short watercourses.
Flood hazard simulations were validated against historical flood marks and spatial extents. Insured claims data for selected events were extracted at address resolution. Damage rate curves linking water flow/depth to destruction rates (DR = claims paid / insured value) were calibrated for residential, commercial, industrial, and agricultural assets: $TD_r = f(\text{m}^3/\text{s} \text{ or } \text{m})$.
Simulated losses were validated against actual historic claims. Hazard intensity reduction scenarios (10–50% reduction ranges) were then applied to model avoided damages. For example, in the Lez catchment during a 2014-scale flood event, a 50% runoff hazard reduction saves residential property owners ~€1.9M (a 40.45% damage reduction).
Integrating stochastic 400-year rainfall simulations (ARPEGE-Climat) under present and 2050 climate conditions (Moncoulon et al., 2018) allows modeling future average annual losses. Results indicate that in the Lez catchment, NBS must achieve a 35% hazard reduction to offset projected climate change impacts and maintain annual average losses at current levels.
<p class="caption-text">Figure II: Catastrophe model structure.</p>4. Knowledge Integration: Adaptive Planning, New Business Models, and Innovative Sustainable Financing Multidisciplinary knowledge from biophysical, social, and economic analyses across demo sites was synthesized into a global decision-support framework applicable to varying technical, environmental, and socioeconomic contexts.
Complementary tools were developed to integrate evaluation elements, such as a stakeholder engagement protocol guiding problem identification, solution selection, and strategy co-design (Annex 1). This process connected directly into an adaptive planning cycle and a dedicated Natural Assurance Business Canvas to identify revenue streams, blended finance options, impact investments, and performance-based contracts.
4.1. The Adaptive Planning Cycle Grounded in adaptive planning frameworks (Basco-Carrera et al., 2020; van Cauwenbergh et al., 2020), adaptive planning is a structured, iterative decision-making process for managing long-term uncertainty through continuous monitoring and learning. Using study-specific models, Dynamic Adaptive Policy Pathways (DAPP) can be developed to establish flexible long-term strategic plans that commit to short-term actions while defining clear frameworks to adjust future actions as conditions evolve.
4.2. The Natural Assurance Business Model Canvas The Natural Assurance Business Model Canvas (Mayor et al., 2020) adapts traditional conceptual business tools (Osterwalder & Pigneur, 2010) to define value propositions, delivery mechanisms, and financial structures for natural assurance schemes. The NAS Canvas differs in two key ways: First, it structures logic around ecosystem service supply and demand; second, it incorporates pluralistic valuation (Sanders et al., 2016) and relational values (Muraca & Himes, 2018) within the IPBES framework (7)—defined as desirable relationships between nature and people (Díaz et al., 2015). The canvas captures public, collective, and private values, facilitating multi-stakeholder alignment and willingness-to-pay for multifunctional NBS strategies delivering concurrent collective benefits over time (Jiang et al., 2016).
Figure 4: Example of NAS Business Canvas applied to the Lower Danube.
4.3. Financial Framework for Water Security The financial framework for water security (Altamirano et al., 2020) adapts the “Five Case Model” (Smith & Flanagan, 2001) for natural assurance schemes across five analytical dimensions: a) Strategic Case: Demonstrates strategic alignment and a compelling case for change. b) Economic Case: Evaluates investment options (green, hybrid, grey) to identify the most cost-effective solution. c) Commercial Case: Ensures commercial viability and deal structure feasibility for NBS. d) Financial Case: Confirms financial affordability and funding availability. e) Management Case: Verifies delivery capabilities and governance processes, typically led by public authorities directly or indirectly exposed to natural hazards.
NBS face specific adoption barriers, including limited access to capital due to a lack of operational real-world track records needed to build investor confidence and de-risk capital. Making NBS attractive to private and impact investors requires clear value proposition quantification and robust business cases ensuring medium-to-long-term returns. Identifying a project’s “business model”—quantifying value propositions, operational assets/partners, delivery costs, beneficiaries, revenue streams, and blended financing packages covering lifecycle capital, operational, and opportunity costs—is essential for de-risking investor perceptions.
5. Case Study Results: Implementation and Lessons Learned This section highlights key findings from selected large- and small-scale NAIAD case studies: Spangen (Rotterdam) and its replication in Valladolid (Spain), the Lower Danube, the Thames Basin, and Medina del Campo.
5.1. Co-Design Process, Problem Ownership, and Legitimacy: Lower Danube (Romania) Covering a 250 km stretch of the Danube River, the Lower Danube demo focused on floodplain restoration to reduce regional flood and drought risks. Guided by the stakeholder engagement protocol (Annex 1), local/regional authorities, insurers, farmers, and basin managers co-designed risk mitigation strategies. Stakeholders identified NBS—specifically restoring the Potelu Lagoon and Bireț floodplains—as the preferred option. Direct benefits (flood risk reduction and avoided damages) were quantified using CCR’s CAT model.
Indirect co-benefits included local economic development, biodiversity enhancement, soil erosion control, and reduced rural-to-urban migration. Through structured co-design, stakeholders mapped problem ownership, implementation responsibilities, regulatory frameworks, direct/indirect beneficiaries (via the NAS Canvas), and capital/O&M cost estimates. Key operational requirements identified included data sharing, governance adaptation, and land-use regulatory revisions. Monitoring indicators were established to track long-term risk reduction and co-benefit delivery.
5.2. NBS Effectiveness: Comparing Flood and Drought Options in the Lower Thames (UK) The Eco:Actuary tool was co-developed with the insurance industry and applied in the Thames Basin alongside local authorities and landowners. NAIAD facilitated engagements with green finance investors exploring Natural Flood Management (NFM) and drought-resilient agricultural practices (e.g., regenerative agriculture), using //Smart: systems to quantify risk reduction. Actuarial associations explored developing a global climate risk index based on Eco:Actuary. Additionally, a UK water utility invested in NAIAD //Smart: technology to guide farmers on soil tillage and cover crop techniques to reduce nitrate leaching and soil erosion across drought-prone chalk aquifers.
Evaluation results confirmed that investing in regenerative agriculture represents the most cost-effective strategy for drought mitigation. Increasing soil infiltration retains water on-site, effectively mitigating downstream flood risks while maintaining water availability during dry seasons. Regenerative farming delivers multiple co-benefits: reduced tillage carbon emissions, enhanced soil organic matter, increased biodiversity, and reduced agricultural runoff pollution.
5.3. Policy Contextualization: Policy Guidelines for Water Security in Medina del Campo (Spain) The Medina del Campo study addressed overexploited aquifer risks under the Groundwater Directive (2006/118/EC) and Water Framework Directive (2000/60/EC), which mandate the Duero River Basin Authority (CHD) to achieve good groundwater status by 2027. Primary pressures include declining water tables, diffuse agricultural nitrate ($NO_3$) pollution, and natural arsenic contamination. CHD’s initial intervention involved surface water transfers from the Adaja River and Cogotas Reservoir to replace groundwater abstraction across 6,000 hectares of irrigated farmland, successfully driving local piezometric recovery by halting abstractions and increasing surface irrigation recharge.
NAIAD supported CHD in identifying and evaluating NAS strategies combining NBS and soft measures to mitigate risks and restore aquifer functionality. Following the stakeholder engagement protocol (Annex 1), CHD assessed technical and legal feasibility for two drought-resilient NAS strategies:
Crop Switching & Conservation: Promoting drought-resistant crop varieties, soil/water conservation practices, water user associations, abstraction monitoring, and environmental awareness. Managed Aquifer Recharge (MAR): Combining artificial recharge infrastructure, water user associations, abstraction control, and public education. Groundwater flow was simulated under three climate scenarios and three management regimes: 1) Business-As-Usual (BAU); 2) Exploitation Index (EI) reduction to 0.85 by 2050; and 3) EI reduction to 0.80 by 2050 (CHD target). Results demonstrated that groundwater management (EI reduction) exerts a significantly greater impact on piezometric recovery than climate-driven recharge changes.
Economic evaluations of both strategies were conducted using Le Coent et al. (2020) CBA frameworks. Socioeconomic and regulatory scenarios incorporated stakeholder-identified drivers, notably European Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) subsidy evolutions (comparing current CAP against eco-directed CAP scenarios). Climate projections (IPCC RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5) showed no statistically significant mean annual rainfall trends for 2050 (CEDEX, 2012; Llorente et al., 2018), leading to baseline historic trend simulations (Calatrava et al., 2019).
Economic impacts were modeled using a calibrated agro-economic tool simulating land and water allocation across crop alternatives. Non-monetized co-benefits were evaluated qualitatively and quantitatively, indicating gains in water productivity, agricultural employment, and farm income. Environmentally, both strategies improved aquifer quantitative/qualitative status, though Strategy 2 (MAR) accelerated recovery and benefited riverine ecosystems, while Strategy 1 promoted lower-intensity farming through crop rotation.
Economic evaluations confirmed that Strategy 1 benefits far exceeded costs (Benefit-Cost Ratio = 3.17), even excluding indirect co-benefits (Calatrava et al., 2019). Strategy 2 enhanced local riverine ecosystems without directly reducing agricultural drought risk. However, Strategies 1 and 2 are highly complementary; combining them accelerates aquifer recovery while maximizing environmental co-benefits, underscoring the necessity of integrated valuation frameworks (López-Gunn et al., 2020).
5.4. Replication: Climate-Resilient Stadiums via NBS—Rotterdam Flood Mitigation and Valladolid Drought Resilience NAIAD’s smallest demo site evaluated neighborhood flood mitigation in Spangen (Rotterdam), where an NBS was installed to increase stormwater retention and relieve sewer overflow pressures during extreme rainfall events. The neighborhood suffered from insufficient retention capacity and drought-related vulnerabilities (urban heat stress, wooden pile foundation degradation). Rotterdam City Council identified a required retention deficit of $53,000\text{ m}^3$.
To address this, the city implemented an “Urban Water Buffer” (UWB) pilot around Sparta Rotterdam’s football stadium. The UWB captures, treats, and stores rainwater runoff from the stadium roof and surrounding streets in subsurface aquifers for pitch irrigation. The system adds $1,500\text{ m}^3$ of retention capacity every 48 hours, simultaneously mitigating flood and drought risks.
NAIAD conducted an economic evaluation comparing three neighborhood-wide flood mitigation strategies:
Grey: Separate sewer systems and permeable paving. Hybrid: Separate sewers combined with natural retention, public square infiltration, and aquifer storage. Green: Exclusive reliance on green retention and infiltration infrastructure. The CBA evaluated direct flood mitigation alongside indirect co-benefits (health impacts, property value appreciation, heat island mitigation, green roof lifespan extension, and potable water savings via reuse).
Results demonstrated that grey solution implementation costs were 15% higher than green NBS for equivalent risk reduction, confirming NBS cost-effectiveness. Furthermore, estimated green co-benefits far exceeded direct flood mitigation value, presenting a compelling investment case.
This solution is currently being replicated at the José Zorrilla football stadium in Valladolid (Spain), combining resources with the Horizon 2020 UrbanGreenUp project, funding from the Dutch Partners for Water innovation fund and Valladolid City Council, and technical support from local water utility Aquavall, Real Valladolid C.F., and the Duero River Basin Authority. This demonstrates how multi-stakeholder partnerships between municipalities, sports clubs, water utilities, basin agencies, European startups, and research institutions can deploy NBS to mitigate flood and drought risks while generating substantial co-benefits.
6. Policy Uptake and Exploitation NAIAD demonstrated the potential of NBS and green infrastructure as future-proof investments for climate adaptation and flood/drought resilience across urban and catchment scales. Resilience gains are built upon avoided damages and natural co-benefits. By introducing Natural Assurance Schemes (NAS), cities and regions can leverage standardized tools: Eco:Actuary and FEV for biophysical assessment, participatory modeling for stakeholder risk perception, integrated CBA, adaptive planning pathways, the NAS Business Model Canvas, and water security financial frameworks.
During the final demo meeting in Copenhagen (January 2020), a simulated investor pitch brought together real public and private investors to identify requirements for converting technical knowledge into bankable NAS projects.
Policy roundtables were conducted across European countries (Spain, France, Romania, Sweden, Slovakia) to validate findings and align results with major European policy initiatives, including the EU Climate Adaptation Strategy, the European Climate Law, and the EU Sustainable Finance Taxonomy. Discussions with the European Commission (DG CLIMA) focused on deploying NBS and NAS to address three critical policy gaps: the protection gap, the investment gap, and the information-sharing gap.
NAIAD provided an integrated conceptual framework and toolkit to quantify ecosystem assurance values across 9 European demo sites spanning diverse scales and implementation stages. These frameworks support embedding NAS into river basin management and restoration planning. Project outputs include open-access training materials for an online MOOC course and an upcoming academic volume published by Springer.
7. Conclusions After more than three years of research, NAIAD provides definitive answers to core disaster management questions:
First, in the context of climate change, land-use shifts, and expanding asset exposure, disaster damages are escalating rapidly—challenging governments, local authorities, insurers, and citizens. Are NBS effective solutions? Can natural assurance schemes improve preparedness while reducing potential costs? Based on project evidence, the answer is unequivocally affirmative.
Second, NAIAD demonstrates that NBS represent vital components of risk reduction portfolios, enhancing systemic resilience while delivering societal co-benefits. However, NBS are not silver bullets; combining NBS with grey infrastructure in hybrid configurations often represents the optimal choice. Developing tailored local solutions requires real-world testing and empirical review. Multidisciplinary integration is essential to address complex hydrological challenges. Simulations indicate that NBS are exceptionally effective at mitigating frequent, lower-magnitude events, thereby elevating baseline system resilience and maximizing prevention-phase assurance values.
Third, standardized NAS evaluation tools facilitate embedding green solutions into river basin management, flood/drought risk planning, and capital allocation—shifting the risk management paradigm toward proactive prevention.
Finally, a major lesson learned involves identifying and resolving stakeholder barriers, particularly surrounding risk perception ambiguity. Mobilizing collective action requires unpacking “transaction costs” to unlock collective risk reduction powered by the inherent protective value of nature.

Annex 1. Stakeholder Engagement Protocol: Co-Designing Natural Assurance Schemes In parallel with technical analyses, multiple local stakeholder workshops were conducted across demo sites. NAIAD partners co-developed identical implementation steps alongside local stakeholders to support effective NBS deployment.
Workshop deliverables included:
Local risk perception evaluation. Selection and validation of optimal solutions (including grey and hybrid measures). Identification of associated co-benefits. Co-definition of long-term monitoring indicators to evaluate risk reduction performance and co-benefit delivery. Detailed analysis of NBS strategies and optimal multi-measure combinations. Final workshop co-identification of potential business models for chosen solutions. A core operational principle of NAIAD is proactive engagement with local stakeholders across study cases throughout conceptual and evaluative methodology deployments. The interdisciplinary nature of the approach makes it relevant to decision-makers, practitioners, scientists, end-users, and communities. Each group contributes unique insights regarding physical, social, cultural, and economic systems. Stakeholders played a vital role in validating and “road-testing” the tools and methods presented in this article.
Participatory modeling techniques were customized based on contextual realities and specific risks. A standardized “stakeholder engagement protocol” was developed to guide practitioners while ensuring cross-site process consistency.
The protocol comprised ten sequential, iterative steps defining objectives and proposing participatory methodologies for data collection, co-design, modeling, and validation.
Acknowledgments: This project received funding from the European Union’s Horizon 2020 Research and Innovation Program under Grant Agreement No. 730497. We express our gratitude to the Duero River Basin Authority for its strong support.
Furthermore, this document synthesizes work contributed by many NAIAD colleagues, including:

© Bibliothèque historique de la ville de Paris (BHVP), G. Leyris, (http://ibytes.es/blog_inundaciones_de_paris_1910.html) / Creative Commons (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/3.0/es/)
The 1910 Paris flood not only produced serious damage but it had a profound impact on the collective consciousness at the time, bearing in mind the context of enthusiasm for great industrial progress in which it occurred. It is an event which always comes up as a reference point when conversation turns to the danger of the river Seine overflowing, not only as this affects metropolitan Paris but also the whole Île-de-France region1. This is a 100-year flood which had forerunners that had made an exceptional impact, such as that which occurred in 1658 and preceded other floods that were substantial, though not as heavy, such as those in 1924 and 1955. And every time when, within the context of a weather pattern of heavy, prolonged downpours, the Seine begins to rise above a certain flow level in the normal range, thoughts turn back to 1910 and the authorities go on the alert. With good reason.
Such concern is actually very understandable. One could pause to reflect on the extent of the potential damage of a flood such as that in Île-de-France in 1910 on virtually all levels: economic, social, cultural, political, etc., and of course just in human terms if one bears in mind that the region is really France’s core. It is the most populated and wealthiest of the 22 administrative regions, bringing together some 19% of the population of France and accounting for 30% of national GDP (5% of EU’s GDP). The government, most of the larger companies, and the major decision-making and research centres are based within this territory, which is also the world’s top tourist destination and Europe’s second most important focal point for attracting investment.
Against this backdrop, and considering that it is a type of slow flood, with the waters taking over for up to two months, an event such as the one in 1910 would have seriously disrupted the functioning of the machinery of the state and the institutions, as well as the financial, commercial and industrial sectors, and essential services and infrastructure (electricity, transport, water, the food supply, telecommunications, public safety, education, etc.) Some five million citizens would find their daily lives significantly affected, especially the 830,000 people living within the area susceptible to flooding, where 55,700 companies are located. All of this is without forgetting the major risk faced by a universal and priceless cultural heritage.
In the worst-case scenario the direct economic damage could be as much as 30 billion euros, while the macroeconomic damage would mean a reduction in GDP (over a period of about five years) of up to 58.5 billion euros, which amounts to a cumulative 3%. In such an extreme case the impact on the operations of companies would imply a toll of 400,000 job-losses.
All of these are reference figures offered in this OECD study to emphasize the pressing need to establish the suitable strategies and public policy for action, in order to reduce in this region the flood risk in the medium and long term via preventive measures, stepping up resilience and reducing vulnerability. This is a goal that has thus far not been possible to achieve satisfactorily. The fact is that, as the study says, the great floods in megacities illustrate the difficulties experienced by societies in striking a balance between development and dealing with the vulnerability associated with the multifaceted exposure of social and economic stakeholders
Protection-oriented efforts (structural measures) have been made since 1910, but investments in this sense have not been forthcoming in any great quantity in recent decades. Meanwhile, vulnerability has been exacerbated by the effect of increasing development activity, the building of critical infrastructure and the greater interdependence of all this, as well as the concentration of assets and people.
The book provides an analysis and recommendations regarding public policy to enhance flood prevention in Île-de-France via the implementation of an ambitious and coherent strategy to manage flood risk in this territory. There is no shortage in France of legislation and schemes purpose-designed for the area of prevention, quite apart from other regulations particularly affecting this region of France, but they will not be wholly effective or become as efficient as they might be if special emphasis is not placed on governance.
The fact is that, as the study says, the great floods in megacities illustrate the difficulties experienced by societies in striking a balance between development and dealing with the vulnerability associated with the multifaceted exposure of social and economic stakeholders (page 36).
And if it is to be effective such policy must be based on a clear definition of the duties and obligations of each of the actors on the stage (institutions and public bodies on the various levels of government, the private sector and civil society), as well as on a coordination of these, backed by incentives, yet also sanctioning, mechanisms. The key points of governance concern the coherence of the legal and regulatory framework and the mandate of the institutions in the service of an established strategy in common, as well as the effective coordination and cooperation among the various stakeholders in executing this.
The second chapter deals with governance, while the third centres on how to bolster resilience in Île-de-France via prevention, not only through using structural measures, where the problem of how to finance these has a decisive bearing, but also non-structural measures, highlighting the importance of awareness of the risk, evaluating it, disseminating information about it, and fostering a risk culture.
Chapter five is given over to funding efforts to enhance resilience, mentioning local and national means to do this. Notable among the former is the scheme for natural catastrophe compensation, created in 1982 and based on a system of reinsurance managed by CCR (Caisse Céntrale de Réassurance), which is backed by the State guarantee.
To summarise, this is a study which uses a holistic approach in examining the problem of managing flood risk in a specific territory, in this case Île-de-France, but which represents a general challenge for all of the great urban sprawls, which must find a solution to striking a balance between developing and controlling vulnerability.
OECD (2014), Seine Basin, Île-de-France 2014: Resilience to Major Floods, OECD Publishing.

Île-de-France is one of the 22 administrative regions within the territory of metropolitan France. Paris is located inside it, for which reason it is also known as the ‘Paris Region’. ↩︎

Two papers are presented here from The Policy Research Working Papers series, prepared in the framework of the Disaster Risk Financing and Insurance Program (DRFIP) of the World Bank Group - Finance and Markets Global Practice Group and published in June 2016. The aim of this working group is to encourage an exchange of ideas on economic development issues.
The Policy Research Working Paper 7720 Solving commitment problems in disaster risk finance D.J. Clarke and L. Wren-Lewis
The initial premise of this paper is that, in the event of a natural catastrophe, the population does not receive the aid it needs. Three causes have been indentified: the first is that households tend to be under-protected in the face of natural disasters –either when taking out insurance or when putting material resources into place for mitigating the consequences– because they are confident that, if a catastrophe occurs, they will receive assistance from governments and private institutions (the Samaritan dilemma). Moreover, the reality of such situations shows that, often, the support arrives late and, due to political corruption and illegitimate interests of the private institutions donating the aid, the relief is misallocated and not distributed in proportion to the damage suffered, reaching the point where some people receive assistance who have not undergone any loss at all.
It is assumed that these problems do not arise –or do so to a lesser degree– in developed countries where the “reputation” of the donors –governments or private institutions– precludes failure to fulfil promises and where there is a separation of powers making it technically impossible to avoid meeting commitments.
According to the authors, the root of the three problems lies in the incapacity of the donors to put their prior commitments into practice, and they propose transferring the risk to third parties as the solution, either through insurance or by using risk transfer financial instruments, such as catastrophe bonds or swaps. The paper also makes a detailed analysis of how and when each kind of instrument should be used in order to prevent over-selling, as if it were a miracle cure against disasters.
The authors support themselves on a model based on the behaviour of recipients (those affected by the catastrophe) and benefactors (the donors of the relief) in order to demonstrate the following propositions:
Proposition 1. When people perceive that, in the event of a catastrophe, they will receive aid from an institution, the recipient will not invest in self-protection, even when it would be clearly beneficial to do so. This will lead to insufficient relief, except in those cases where the benefactor is absolutely altruistic.
Proposition 2. Benefactors are more willing to invest money in preventing the inadequate allocation of aid before a disaster strikes, for example, by establishing rigorous auditing mechanisms capable of preventing corruption at any point in the chain of distribution of the relief.
For this reason, it is more effective if donors commit to providing aid prior to a catastrophe than after it has occurred.
Proposition 3. Benefactors take longer in disbursing aid if the number of donors is sufficiently large.
One way of avoiding this tendency would be for each benefactor to unilaterally commit to providing the relief as soon as possible, regardless of what the rest may do.
The final conclusion reached is that a natural disaster relief system based on the generosity of individuals or institutions is inefficient in practice.
The authors of the paper have examined a number of measures that relief donors could adopt to improve the efficiency of the system:
1. Transfer the risk to third parties, either by subsidising the insuring of the recipient or by taking out insurance themselves instead of handing over post-disaster cash.
Making insurance by the recipient compulsory –the laws of some countries establish this obligation– is an incentive for recipients to take measures for mitigating losses (thereby preventing the Samaritan dilemma), since the insurance premium is established in relation to the risk. In addition, the insuring of the benefactor eliminates the possible increase in the marginal cost of seeking post-disaster financing.
Moreover, involving the insurance sector would help to solve the problem of corruption in the allocation of the relief, because the sector would be the first to be concerned with ensuring that the compensation paid is received solely by those who have suffered losses. Likewise, this would drive donors to provide truthful information on the losses.
Finally, the payments would arrive on schedule without delays due to the re-negotiation of the aid by donors after the loss has occurred.
2. Integrate the information systems on the payments made. Adopting common systems could prevent the lack of commitment on the part of some donors to collect or disclose accurate information on losses from rendering the relief system inefficient. Once again, the insurance companies would be the first to have an interest in seeing the system operate effectively, in order to maintain the confidence of their insured.
3. Use “disaster indices”, which are basically statistics built on the basis of objective data (for example, data supplied by weather satellites or seismic stations), correlating them with the loss data. This eliminates, in part, the problem of the misallocation of the relief due to the corruption of intermediaries, since an index is less vulnerable to manipulation than mere data on losses, as it is supported on a technology which is more difficult to falsify.
The Policy Research Working Paper 7721 Evaluating sovereign disaster risk finance strategies. A framework D. Clarke, O. Mahul, R. Poulter and T.L. Teh
This paper analyses the financial instruments available to governments for meeting the costs of the losses caused by climatic catastrophes on a national scale. The aim of the study is to facilitate the choice between one financing strategy and another depending on the real risk of disaster, economic conditions and political constraints of the hypothetically affected country, in such a way as to reduce the cost for the national budget as far as possible.
In addition, it develops a quantitative method for determining a strategy that will minimise the average cost or minimise the cost of disasters above a given return period (of a particular magnitude).
To do so, the authors use a quantitative method built in two stages, where the government can choose one or several strategies for financing possible losses (x) up to a maximum amount (X). The strategies examined are:
risk transfer instruments, such as parametric insurance and catastrophe bonds or swaps; budget provisions for financing possible losses; post-disaster emergency budget reallocations; and post-disaster lines of credit or loans. Phase 1 (prior to the occurrence of the event): the government chooses the maximum amount to be financed with each instrument ($L_j$) which it will not be able to change once the actual amount of the losses is known.
Phase 2 (subsequent to the occurrence of the event): once the amount of the losses is known, the government can choose what amount $l_j(x)$ it will finance through each instrument chosen in Phase 1, on the condition that the amount $L_j$ fixed in the first phase cannot be exceeded. That is, $l_j(x) \le L_j$ for all $j$ and $x$.
The model must be actuarially “sound”. That is, that the sum of what is obtained with each instrument is effectively equal to the amount intended to be financed– $\sum l_j(x) = x$ for all $x$.
A layered financing strategy is established where each layer is the amount financed through a specific instrument, in the understanding that the next layer will not be used until the previous layer has been exhausted.
Each of the instruments proposed is evaluated according to its financial particularities using the notion of opportunity cost of each ($C_j x$), understanding as such the economic cost involved in using that instrument $j$ in the financing of the expenses $x$.
The outline of the model is presented on a table where each financial instrument is characterised in relation to two constants $a$ and $b$ –called cost parameters– which are mathematical proportions between their financial parameters (interest rate, premiums, etc.).
The conclusion, stated in the form of a theorem, is the following:
“If a government wishes to minimise the financing costs of disaster relief, it should use a layered loss financing strategy, where the xth unit of expenditure will be financed by the instrument $j$ with the smallest relation $a_j + b_j (1-F(z))$ [where $1-F(z)$ is the likelihood of exceeding a given cost $z$ and $a_j$ and $b_j$ are the cost parameters of the instrument $j$].”
To set the ideas in a context, at the end of the study, the methodology is applied to a specific example, a hypothetical country with a set of given characteristics. The example shows that, obviously, the pre-existing economic situation and the type of risk to be addressed are key elements for determining the most cost-effective financing structure.
The conclusion of the study is that using a combination of different financial instruments is the most efficient manner from the opportunity-cost perspective for financing the amount earmarked for paying for the disaster relief.
In addition, there are other aspects, which are not of a quantitative nature and therefore do not arise as a conclusion of the study, but which do have an influence in favour of the use of risk transfer instruments, such as insurance. Insurance can solve the commitment problems faced by governments, enabling them to implement better-focussed responses quicker and without the need for the backing of powerful administrations from the financial point of view.
References Clarke, Daniel Jonathan; Wren-Lewis, Liam (2016) Solving commitment problems in disaster risk finance. Policy Research working paper; no. WPS 7720. Washington, D.C.: World Bank Group. http://documents.worldbank.org/curated/en/396511468197075071/Solving-commitment-problems-in-disaster-risk-finance Clarke, Daniel Jonathan; Mahul, Olivier; Poulter, Richard Andrew; Teh, Tse-Ling (2016) Evaluating sovereign disaster risk finance strategies : a framework. Policy Research working paper; no. WPS 7721. Washington, D.C. : World Bank Group. http://documents.worldbank.org/curated/en/430111468184437717/Evaluating-sovereign-disaster-risk-finance-strategies-a-framework
